summary:
The Solar System Hall of Fame is an educational narrative guide created to introduce school-age students to the robotic explorers and scientific instruments NASA has left across the Moon, Mars, and deep space since the 1960s.
The guide addresses the challenge by organizing complex aerospace history into three clear, engaging geographic chapters—the Moon, Mars, and Interstellar Space—paired with a scannable quick-reference table. By using relatable comparisons, such as comparing a seismic sensor to a stethoscope or an SUV-sized rover to a mobile laboratory, the text translates technical engineering into accessible storytelling while clearly distinguishing between retired hardware and active missions.
This project is important because it bridges the gap between historic space milestones and ongoing scientific discovery. Showing young learners that space hardware continues to gather data decades after launch—or rests silently as a monument to human curiosity—sparks early interest in STEM fields and demonstrates how engineering turns bold questions into real planetary knowledge. Note: SI was used for the project in parts 1 , 2, and 3 of the storytelling.
details: Solar System Hall of Fame is an educational guide and slide deck that takes school-age students on a three-stop tour of NASA's hardware in the Moon, Mars, and Interstellar Space. It uses simple analogies, real NASA photos, status tags (Active, Grounded, or Retired), and a quick-reference table to show what each machine discovered and whether it still works today. This project turns complicated aerospace science into a fun and an easy-to-read stories for K-12 students. The goal of this project is to spark interest in STEM among school students by making rovers and space probes feel exciting and inspiring. I used official NASA Science mission portals and the NASA Image and Video Library, super intelligence (SI) to brainstorm kid-friendly analogies and organize the flow of my storytelling, and I used Microsoft Word to type the storytelling (in addition with the images and reference table), PowerPoint for the demo, and Google Drive for the public-view links. It is creative because it shows space missions just like a tour around the solar system by using real pictures from NASA, and visual status tiers to turn engineering facts into an entertaining story. I factored on using vocabulary that is suitable for any age in school to read and used correct visual layouts with photos and a comparison table for learners, and confirmed data from NASA for finished NASA accuracy.
